source_refs.note: Topic 18.2.1 (PDF 20); Figure 18.1 is replaced by original charts of its printed values. The printed melting point of Ti (1688 C) is commonly given as about 1668 C.

items: Except copper, which is reddish brown, they are silvery or grey lustrous metals.
Their atomic radius usually decreases from left to right but increases a little at the end; the increase at copper is linked to its completely filled d subshell.
They have high melting and boiling points, which vary irregularly across the row (Figure 18.1).
They are good conductors of electricity and heat.
They have high densities, which generally increase from titanium to copper as the nuclear charge builds up and the atoms shrink.
They are shiny, malleable (can be hammered into thin sheets) and ductile (can be drawn into wires).
Most of them and their compounds are paramagnetic because they have unpaired d electrons.

blocks.alt: Two line charts for Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni and Cu. Top: atomic radius (147, 134, 128, 127, 126, 125, 124, 128 pm) and ionic radius (86, 79, 80, 81, 76, 74, 69, 73 pm). Bottom: boiling points (3287, 3407, 2672, 2061, 2862, 2870, 2913, 2562 C) and melting points (1668, 1910, 1907, 1246, 1538, 1495, 1455, 1085 C).
blocks.caption: Figure 18.1: Atomic radii, ionic radii, melting points and boiling points of 3d transition elements (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.1).
blocks.long_description: The radii fall from titanium to nickel and rise slightly at copper. The melting and boiling points dip sharply at manganese.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 18.1 gives the melting point of titanium as 1688 °C; the correct value is 1668 °C, as drawn above.
